MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT AND NATIONAL DEFENCE TAX-REFERENCES TO "GLOBE AND MAIL*' EDITORIAL
Mr. J. L. O'BRIEN (Northumberland, N.B.):	On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker: on May 15, when the national defence tax was being discussed in this house I made reference to the method by which it was deducted from the indemnity of members. At that time I said, as reported at page 2850 of Hansard:
Now that we are pondering the problems of those in the lower income 'brackets, it seems to me that we should attempt to unscramble our
[Mr. Pouliot.l
own positions as members of parliament. We, of course, have to pay the national defence tax, and I wish it to be clearly understood that I am not objecting to paying that tax, but I am objecting to the method by which the tax is collected.
I quote the following from the editorial page of the Toronto Globe and Mail of May 19:
Members of parliament will pay national defence tax on their sessional indemnities. They'd better. Such exemption-and it has been discussed-would be for the average taxpayer about the last straw.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that from my remarks no such implication could properly be attached to any hon. member of this house. I made my point crystal clear-that I was not objecting to the deduction, but only to the method used to deduct it, in that an indemnity is not a salary.
The Globe and Mail item does not mention my name, but since I was the only member making such a reference I here and now protest against statements of members of this house being twisted by any editor in order to attempt further to lower the standing of members of this house in the public opinion by implying that they seek to avoid their obligations.

On a further question of privilege relating to the same article, which said the members of parliament will pay, it should have read that members of parliament "have been paying" the national defence tax.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: REPRESENTATION OF GOVERNMENT IN DRAFTING OF CONTRACT
speechtext:
Yesterday I answered verbally a
question asked by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot). The latter part of my answer related to a question the purpose of which, the hon. member explained, was to inquire as to who represented the government in connection with the drafting of the Bren gun contract. I replied at that time to the effect that the government was represented by the judge advocate general and by the officials of the Department of Justice. I spoke from memory; as a matter of fact I had not understood the hon. member's question. But last night I had the matter checked up, and I find that I was quite in error in my reference to the officials of the Department of Justice. What I find is that the judge advocate general himself represented the department in connection with the contract, and that he did not consult the Department of Justice about this particular contract. What the judge advocate said, and what I must have had in my mind, was that there was a clause in this contract which was similar to a clause in previous contracts, about which clause he had consulted the Department of Justice, and as I remember, what he said was that he considered that what was good enough for the Department of Justice was good enough for him to insert in the contract.
I regret the error and hasten to correct it.

speakerposition: stagedirection

speechtext: I am opposed to this resolution, just the same as I was opposed to Bennett's social legislation. I am opposed to it in its entirety, and if I do not speak on every resolution called, it does not mean that I am not against it. I am against this piece of legislation from the first to the last, for reasons stated yesterday and for other reasons I could give in proper time. It is bad, rotten and dangerous legislation.

Paragraph (a) of resolution 2 refers to "property transferred by the deceased in his lifetime in contemplation of death." Does the federal department intend to proceed as the Ontario government has done, and search bank accounts for thirty years back? As to the expression "contemplation of death," every man contemplates death. How far back is the government going?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot say how far back the investigations will go, but if I am correctly informed, in Ontario gifts made many years ago are deemed to be property passing on the death, whether made in contemplation of death or not. Under this resolution, for a gift simply to be recorded as property passing on the death it must have been made within three years before the death.
Would it not be wise to put in paragraph (a) an addition indicating that -this would go back only three years?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; this is an entirely different thing. The gift to be regarded as property passing on the death must be made after April 29, if I remember correctly. But gifts are not covered by paragraph (a) of section 2. That paragraph covers something else, namely, property transferred by the deceased in his lifetime in contemplation of death. It would include some gifts, but something more than gifts is required under paragraph (a); it must be a gift -made in contemplation of death. That is regarded as property passing on the death, even though it may be made many years before such death.

Then the government could go back even thirty years? The Ontario government has done that, and it does not seem fair.
Succession Duty Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As I said before, the hon. member is talking about something which is different.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, he is talking about gifts made, whether in contemplation of death or otherwise. I am quite sure that under the Ontario act gifts are regarded as property passing on the death, even though they were made many years ago. I believe that those are the investigations to which the hon. member refers. The instances in connection with property transferred by a deceased in his lifetime in contemplation of death would be very few in number, and it would be extremely difficult to prove what was transferred or made in contemplation of death unless it were done comparatively recently. But there is no limitation as to time.

Resolution 2 (g) refers to "annuities or other interests purchased or provided by the deceased to the extent of the beneficial interest arising on his death." It would seem that a tax is here to be paid in respect of succession duties, both on capital and on interest, in addition to income tax. It is true that annuities are taxable under the income tax legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

And according to this resolution they are again taxable under the succession duty provisions. Is there not some conflict in regard to what is capital in the passing and what is income? It seems to me that only the interest on annuities should be subject to income tax, or there should be no tax on the annuities.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The annuities taxed here
are those beginning at the date of death. They are annuities after the death, payable to someone after the decease. The deceased is not taxed on those for income tax.
Is there not double taxation here?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
It looks as if the government is taxing the succession in the form of succession duty and then taxing it again by way of income from year to year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct. If $100,000 passed to a beneficiary he would be taxed on the $100,000 under the Succession Duties Act, and he would be taxed on the income from that $100,000, as the years went by, by way of income tax.	'

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Resolution agreed to.

Do "funeral expenses"
include medical expenses prior to death?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Ordinarily medical expenses would be included in debts. Funeral expenses and debts may be deducted. The amount owing to the doctor would be a debt.

Yesterday the leader of the opposition raised a question in respect of an estate being mulcted once, twice, or three times in rapid succession, in the event of deaths. I am not sure whether the minister gave a final answer. He will be aware of instances in other countries-I am thinking of one or two cases in the United Kingdom which have come to my knowledge-when two and even three deaths in less than two years have played havoc with the property distributed under the terms of a will.
Mr. ILSLEY': No provision is made in these resolutions, nor do I think there is any in the bill to afford relief against several impositions of succession duties at short intervals, or what are called quick successions. The matter could perhaps be considered before the bill is introduced, but as at present prepared there is no such clause. In that regard I believe it is similar to many other succession duties acts.
Under the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act there is power to remit penalties and duties and amounts due the crown. That power is used very sparingly. It is exercised only in well-recognized classes of cases. It is very rarely indeed that an exception is made to the rules laid down, but that power does exist in the crown and could be utilized if it were considered proper to do so in order to relieve a particular case.
It seems to me that it would be well worth serious consideration. As the minister says, the need would not arise often, but it would be wise to make provision for it in the act.

I take a somewhat opposite view. I think the proposals now before us are modest compared with succession duties

Succession Duty Act
elsewhere, and in no event would any great hardship be imposed upon an estate under this particular resolution even if there were three or four deaths in quick succession. Even if the imposition were much heavier, in my opinion death duties are long overdue in this country. They provide a method of distributing wealth which under modern circumstances is very badly needed. This legislation is to be commended, and I do not think we should give the government power to vary it on any grounds.
The one piles on top of the other.

I have in mind a case that occurred in a city in Ontario. I shall not mention the place, because many would know the estate to which I refer. The father, the head of the house, died. At the time of his death he was operating a large plant which employed five or six hundred men. Most of his estate was left to his son. Shortly afterwards, apparently not too long afterwards, the son also passed away and another succession duty had to be paid. This resulted in the closing of the plant and the throwing out of employment of a number of men. Surely my hon. friend to my left would not be in accord with anything like that. This may be an extreme case, but perhaps the regulations should be such as to prevent such a plant being closed up because of two or three taxes being imposed in quick succession.
Will funeral expenses cover a lot in the cemetery and a tombstone?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The commissioner informs me that it is intended that a suitable monument would be included in the funeral expenses. I do not believe the term "funeral expenses" is defined in the bill. When the bill itself is before us I think it will be found that some of these things are provided for.
I am obliged to the hon. gentleman for bringing to my attention this case of quick succession, and also to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) for expressing his views. It shows the difficulty that a moderate, sane government faces when attempting to meet all views. I should think the reasonable course to follow is to make no provision at all in the bill. In another year's time we shall know what our experience is. Under the Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act there is power to grant by order in council relief in such cases if it is considered desirable so to do. I am not saying that it is desirable, and it might be that years would go by before such a case would arise. At such time relief can be granted by order in council, or we can come to the house and state the case and propose an amendment.

In the case I mentioned the succession duties were somewhere around $100,000 upon the decease of the head of the family. The son took over the plant, but he died within a short time and the two succession duties ruined the estate so far as the plant was concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The question that arises is whether power should be given by the bill to the governor in council, apart from the powers it already possesses, to deal with such cases and if so, with what limitations, or whether the whole matter should be dealt with legislatively. I understand that in some acts it is provided that a portion, perhaps half the succession duty, is payable should certain conditions exist. I am not prepared to insert such a clause in this measure. It may be different from the other acts; it may be different in its incidence, and it may be that that would be improper for this act while it is proper for others.

In many cases, particularly where the estate is small, the husband will leave his whole estate to his wife and nothing to the children. The wife may die in a few years, as happens quite often when she is about the same age as the husband. Then the estate is subject to double succession duties, which would be in addition to the provincial duties. This makes the tax very high in the aggregate. Those of moderate means who do not consult solicitors or notaries when drawing their wills do not realize that they can leave a life interest to their widow and have the property pass on to the children upon her death. This is of some consequence to people in moderate circumstances who quite often draw their own holograph wills, and the result is that in a few years the estate is subject to two or more succession duties. This point should be considered if the minister will not consider some amelioration of the tax itself.

In considering hardships
that may arise in connection with quick succession matters, I suggest to the minister that one form of relief which ought to be considered in dealing with estates such as the one mentioned by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) is to give the commissioner authority to receive the succession duty on the second estate in instalments over a period of years with interest at, say, three per cent. This would enable a going concern to carry on. Such a firm would be required to pledge its assets primarily to the department to ensure payment over a period of years. I think this would cure the difficulty. Like the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, I am opposed to any exemption on
Succession Duty Act

the second or even the third estate when quick succession occurs. In the case instanced by the hon. member for Davenport, the man apparently was able to employ 500 men, and the hon. member said that the succession duties were very large. On the theory ot having an eye to what is left, there would even in that case be plenty left for those who take an unearned increment which falls into their lap by devolution. My suggestion is that by giving power to amortize over a period the succession duty to be paid we would do away with the hardship and protect the country so far as insistence on payment of death duties is concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will bear in mind what my hon. friend has said. A bill will be placed before the house, of course, when the resolutions are through, and I think it contains a provision which meets substantially the views my hon. friend has just expressed. Some hon. members have suggested that all imports from the United Kingdom be given free entry into Canada. The government does not propose to adopt such a course, because our objective is to grant concessions which will enable British goods to remain competitive without reducing revenue duties more than necessary.
It is proposed to retain the full rates of duty on alcoholic beverages, primarily because it is not desired to sacrifice revenue on these goods. Other considerations are the inadvisability of stimulating consumption and the fact that imports of British liquors have shown no tendency to decline or to be supplanted by imports from outside the sterling area.
Tobacco products and sugar products are not given any concession because they are not normally imported from the United Kingdom in substantial volume and because their production requires the use of imported raw materials which are in short supply in Britain.
To have reduced the duties on silks would have been inconsistent with the restrictions placed on the production of such goods in Canada.
It is believed that a discount of 25 per cent from the British preferential tariff should be adequate to enable British woollens and boots and shoes to remain competitive. These products are not handicapped to the same extent as most with respect to either raw materials or labour, and due to their relatively high value in relation to weight they are affected less by increased transportation costs. Moreover, there has not been apparent any tendency for imports from foreign countries to replace British woollens and boots and shoes in the Canadian market.

speechtext: The information of the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Wood) is entirely correct. That the tax on long distance telephone calls be increased from six per cent of the charge made to ten per cent; provided however that upon long distance telephone calls made from any public pay station there shall be paid in lieu of the tax hereinbefore provided for the sum of five cents for each such call for which a charge of more than twenty-five cents and not more than fifty cents is made and five cents for each additional charge of fifty cents or any fraction of fifty cents; and provided further that the tax imposed shall in no case be greater than fifty cents on any one call.

The working classes of
this country, who utilize the long distance telephone for business and personal matters, are being asked to pay too much by this increase from six to ten per cent. In 1908 the telephone companies were placed under the jurisdiction of the railway commission, but even to-day we have one of these companies coming to parliament and asking for
IMr. Ilsley.]
vast powers. It is well known that there has been no regulation of these telephone rates since the city of Toronto applied some years ago for an order compelling the Bell Telephone company to reduce its charges. The commercial and domestic rates charged by the telephone companies are exorbitant, when one remembers that they are paying huge dividends on stock that is very greatly watered. Residential rates have gone sky high. 1 had an application myself before the railway commission in an endeavour to have those rates reduced. Why, they were charging $60 and $70 for a residence telephone north of Bloor street in Toronto. That city spent over 860,000 for experts who gave evidence at the hearing of the application, and the company was compelled to bring its rates down to a more reasonable level.
To raise this tax from six to ten per cent is beyond all reason. I do not believe this would be done if the government had to pay for the transatlantic telephone calls they make every day, and dear knows they are not accomplishing very much by those calls, if we are to judge by the apologies made in this house every few days. This tax is too high. Our rates do not compare at all well with those charged in other countries, where telephone companies are subject to some sort of regulation. There is no attempt at regulation of the Bell Telephone company in this country at the present time. There has not been even an application for an order reducing the rates, but now the government comes along with a fiat increase in the tax from six to ten per cent. We must remember that this will react on a great many Canadian homes. Between 1921 and 1930 over six hundred thousand people, nearly half of them returned soldiers, were forced to leave this country for which they had fought at the risk of their lives and go to the United States to look for jobs, thanks to the tariff and free trade policies of hon. gentlemen opposite. These people need to telephone home once in a while. Many of these poor people who lived here like their friends at home to telephone them, and now the government comes along and penalizes them by a six to ten per cent nuisance tax.
The government has gone far enough in attacking in this way the working classes of this country, and in loading up the budget in order to save the dollar. This tax will be passed on to these people to pay. If only the government had been as busy, through its great diplomats at Washington, something might have been done to help us. China can get relief, but Canada can get no relief under the lease-lend bill. As one prominent man

has said, after all it is only a lend and lease measure, and some day someone will have to pay for it. If Canada had skilled negotiators at Washington, we would not have items in the budget like this. We would not have nearly a billion dollars in the .estimates, because the United States would have to pay for the defence which this country is giving them, and which the mother country gave them for two hundred years. Parliament might as well adjourn to-morrow for all the good we are doing here. We are sitting here day after day, but we have no control whatever over taxation. We have surrendered our power. Nobody can strike a word or a cent [DOT]off the budget, and I protest, on behalf of the wage-earners. They are the people who will have to pay the bill.
We see what the telephone company do in [DOT]connection with long-distance charges. They name a rate, and then they add toll charges, and a number of other charges. The charges are exorbitant. The railway commission [DOT]could not regulate them. They cannot regulate even a few passes. When this company was placed under the control of the railway commission, it was notified that any application with respect to rates or charges would be submitted to the railway commission, to find *out if such rates or charges were reasonable. I say that they are not reasonable, and that in the cities and towns they are twice what they ought to be.
The hon. member for Peel and the hon. member for Ontario will know that I had an .application before the commission for a flat rate for the whole of greater Toronto and Y'ork county, including what is known as the suburban counties of Peel and Ontario. The rates charged were found to be exorbitant. I protest against this provision. If I am the only person who protests against these rates, then I shall continue to protest against their being charged workers in Canada. Has the minister made any survey of the company? Has he made any survey as to the ability of the people to pay? What are the urban and suburban rates with this tax added? What regulation is there of the rates of the Bell Telephone company, and the other municipal companies which operate under franchises?

The explanation of this resolution is that the new rate of ten per cent on long-distance telephone calls takes the place of the six per cent rate, which has been unchanged since 1932. The tax continues to apply under the new rate only to calls for which the charge is in excess of fifteen cents, as was the case under the former rate.
In the case of calls made from public pay-stations, because of the difficulty involved in collecting a percentage tax, a tax at a flat rate is collected. Under the new rates this flat rate tax is five cents on all calls costing more than twenty-five cents and less than fifty cents, plus five cents for each additional fifty cents or fraction thereof, which compares with the former rate of five cents on all calls costing more than twenty-five cents and less than eighty cents, plus five cents for each additional eighty cents or fraction thereof.
It is estimated that the increased rates of tax will produce 1600.000 additional revenue in a full year, and $550,000 in the remainder of the present fiscal year. The revenue from long-distance telephone calls was $804,218 in 1939-40 and $921,331 in 1940-41.

I think every hon. member is pleased about the announcement made to the house by the minister that the ten per cent tax on transportation will be taken off fares issued to service men.
Could the minister explain why a class which is well able to pay for its transportation should be exempt from the ten per cent tax? Most of those who travel on railway passes are of a class who are in a position to pay. Many of them hold high offices. While I am not one to impose taxation on any group, yet on the other hand I think it most unfair to take the ten per cent tax from those who have to pay for their tickets on steamships, railways or aeroplanes and not take it from those who mostly travel free. Why should that class be exempt?
Does the ruling with respect to the elimination of the ten per cent tax on soldiers' tickets include the tax on tickets purchased by nurses engaged in war work?
Anyone engaged in war work.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Nurses in the armed forces, yes. Then, with regard to passes, I believe the suggestion made by the hon. member for New Westminster reflects great credit upon him. He comes from British Columbia, and the effect of taxing members' passes would be that members from British Columbia would pay in taxes many times the amount of the tax of a member living nearer Ottawa. That is, however, only a small consideration.
The important point is that a large number of pass holders are employees of the railway companies. They assume, and I presume rightly so, that free transportation is part of their remuneration. It is one of the privileges or advantages they have.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It is one of the working conditions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is part of their remuneration or wages. I consider that if we were to begin collecting transportation taxes from these employees of the railway companies, many of whom have to use the railways to go from one place to another, in the discharge of their duties on the railways, we would be following an improper procedure.

That is all very well, but I do not think the minister has looked into the matter as fully as he might. I have in mind classes of railway employees who are well able to pay. I refer to the office class and the superintendent class, and from there up to the president. Those people are in receipt of large salaries. From conversation

with them I know they do not take into account the fact that they travel free, as part of their salaries. This is the class of traveller who is well able to pay. He may step on the train, take his wife and family, and pay no tax; yet the poor traveller who buys a ticket will have to fork out ten per cent as a tax. This is not fair legislation, and, I believe, will bring about a great deal of unrest in the minds of many people. The reason given by the minister is not a just reason why this class should be exempt.

I should like to emphasize a point I made when the budget was under debate. I said that this tax should not be imposed at all. I am not going to enter into any argument about the taxation of somebody else in connection with transportation; but I do not think this tax should be imposed at all, because the people who can afford it have passenger automobiles, and often travel in that way. In many instances those who use our railway and bus systems of transportation are those who have no other way of travel, and who frequently travel of necessity.
The railway fares in this country, a country of great distances, are very high compared with those in other parts of the world. I am firmly of opinion that this tax is wrong in principle because, in a very large degree, it is taxing a group of people who must travel, and who have no means other than the public transportation systems.
I was pleased to hear the minister announce that soldiers in uniform would be relieved of this transportation tax. I am asking him to give some consideration to the point which I have raised and about which I am sure other members feel as I do. If we need to raise money by a tax on transportation, let us impose a heavier tax upon the more luxurious forms of travel such as the compartment, the drawing-room and the chair. Many people have no other means of travel than the railways and bus systems of transportation, and they often travel in search of work or because of sickness or something of that kind. Let us relieve these people of this additional burden. As I said before, Canada is a country of great distances, and the imposition of a tax of this description will be a real hardship upon those groups of people who have no other means of transportation.
I ask the minister to give this particular suggestion further consideration.

I also appreciate the fact that the minister has seen fit to eliminate this tax in so far as soldiers are concerned.
I believe considerable dissatisfaction would have been caused among the troops had that not been done. While we are dealing with this matter, I wish to protest at the failure of the government to provide free passes for embarkation leave and furlough. We all appreciate-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I must rise to a point of order. If we get on to the question of free transportation for soldiers, it will take the rest of the evening.

I was just going to point out that if free transportation had been granted to our soldiers, this question of a tax on their fares would never have arisen. I consider that this proposal to place a ten per cent tax on transportation is a vicious practice. Generally speaking, the burden will not be placed upon those who are best able to pay. The greater proportion of people travelling on trains to-day are either in the exempted class or the lower income brackets. One needs only to pass through a transcontinental train to see how few people there are occupying drawingrooms, to see how few there are in the parlour car, to see the slightly greater number in the tourist car, to see the day coaches crammed full. It is the poorer classes of our people who provide the greater part of the traffic on our railroads, and they are the ones who will have to bear the greater burden under this proposal. I would suggest, as did the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), that there be an increased tax upon the more luxurious forms of travel, such as the standard coaches, drawing-rooms and tourist travel, but no tax whatsoever upon day-coach travel.
If the idea of this tax is to restrict holiday travel, then I (hink the government is making a serious mistake. People suffer a certain amount of nervous tension during war time, and they are more in need of vacations than
in peace time in order to keep up their morale. We all know how hard it is for certain classes of our people, especially our farming classes, to find the money for a holiday. Very often it is a matter of saving for several months in order to scrape together S9 or $10 with which to provide a holiday at the side of a lake. Some of these people are lucky and have cars; others have cars but have no money to buy licences, while others have no money to buy gas. Many of our people must travel by railway, and this ten per cent tax might make it impossible for them to take a holiday.
If the idea of this proposal is to raise revenue, then I am satisfied that there are more equitable means of doing this. If the minister is so much in love with indirect taxation, I can suggest one tax. He should place a tax upon advertising in the press and over the radio. This would accomplish three things. First, it would reduce the amount of labour required to produce the advertising. Second, it would reduce spending, because I think everyone admits that advertising increases spending.
No.
What is the use of advertising if it does not increase spending?
What is the use of having a business if you do not advertise?

Third, it would produce revenue. Time and time again the minister has stressed the point that taxation should be imposed upon those best able to pay. We all know that indirect taxation does not do this; indirect taxation is inequitable and unequal. Direct taxation takes the money from those who have it. The other day I suggested to the minister that instead of having indirect taxation, he should increase the taxation against those people who have money to buy bonds. At that time he protested that a tax of that kind would be in the nature of a capital levy.
I would remind the minister that the surplus income of to-day becomes the capital of to-morrow. The correct time to tax that capital is when it is still income. If, however, we fail to tax that when we should, that is no excuse for our failing to tax it after it becomes capital. So long as we recognize the fact that in many instances that capital has resulted from war profits, then I would not for one minute protest against a capital levy. The excess profits tax could be increased from 75 per cent to 100 per cent, and the taxes upon incomes in the higher brackets could be increased. As has been stressed so many times from this side of the house, it is not the amount a person pays, it is the amount he

has left after his tax has been paid that really matters. People throughout this country are not going to be satisfied simply to be told that the government is going to insist upon the principle of equality of service and sacrifice and place taxation upon those best able to bear it unless the government itself puts that principle into force; and so long as the people have to pay this form of tax and the kind of taxes provided for in the next few resolutions, they are going to feel that the government is laying itself open to the charge of hypocrisy and lack of sincerity.

I imagine that the sole reason for this tax is the raising of revenue, and on that ground I oppose the tax because I believe it will defeat its own ends. For a number of years the railways of Canada have been offering special fares, excursion rates and various other inducements to people to travel. Railway fares will be increased considerably by this ten per cent tax, depending of course upon the distance travelled. I have been living in British Columbia and have had to travel to Ottawa several times a year, and on those train journeys I have seen, as the hon. member for Acadia has pointed out, the large number of people who travel in the day coaches. I have seen women travelling all the way by day coach from British Columbia to some point in eastern Canada. Instead , ' being taxed, they should be paid a bonus foi having to travel in that way. These are the people who, in large measure, will be compelled to pay the increased railway fares.
Again, a large number of the people who travel from one place to another in Canada are travelling to work or to look for work, and the government is charging them an extra ten per cent for travelling.

Special War Revenue Act
As a means of raising revenue, this tax will defeat its own ends because it will curtail railway travel. People in Canada should be encouraged to travel from one point of the country to another whenever possible. That should be a matter of public policy, because people living in one province, in British Columbia, for example, know as little about Nova Scotia or New Brunswick or Quebec as they know about England or Scotland or Ireland. We should make it as easy as possible for people to travel from one part of Canada to another, rather than make it more difficult by taxation, because travelling helps to develop a national consciousness. I know the difficulties of the minister. I do not think he imposed this tax just to be cantankerous or anything of that kind. I know he has to look for money where he can find it, But this is not a logical place to look for it because the tax will fall on people who are already overburdened.

Perhaps I do not agree entirely with the arguments which have just been advanced. If I were the Minister of Finance, I would ask those who are opposing this tax to suggest a substitute tax. Money must be raised, and taxation in some form or another is necessary. I travel a , little, and when I go home over the week-end I think I should pay a tax because I have all the fun and enjoyment of going home instead of staying in the city of Ottawa over the weekend. Anyone who travels on the trains must have noticed that the dining-car is packed at meal time, and any man who can pay $1.25 for a meal can afford to pay tax on his railway ticket. I know that the day coach is well filled too but a good many of the people in the day coach go into the diner. The only reason I could see for not imposing this tax would be the number of workers who have to travel. I am reminded of the old proverb, "a rolling stone gathers no moss." If a man has a job, he does not need to travel from Vancouver to the maritimes to look for work. He can build up his body and mind right at home. I am only one of those who would pay my own fare and have the railway pass lifted rather than have the soldiers taxed when travelling. I am not sure, however, that other travellers should not pay the tax.

I was thinking particularly of people in the western part of this dominion;. In the large open spaces, travelling is quite a problem. In many parts of that area where people are becoming poorer, doctors have moved out, and persons who require medical attention have to travel long distances. The imposition of a ten per cent tax on transportation will involve them in increased hardship. With regard to substituting something which, I believe, would be a suitable alternative, I notice that the government has been very careful not to tax alcoholic liquor. I do not understand why this form of luxury of a certain group of people should not be taxed.
Nobody on the government side uses it.

I believe that between $90 and $100 million a year is spent on liquor in Canada. The government taxes the beer of the working man, but it has made no move to increase the tax on spirituous liquors. There is one part of this resolution which, so far as I know, has not been covered by the minister. I notice that transportation is divided into two classes. With respect to transportation by railway, bus or aircraft one class of words is used, but as regards vessels a different expression is employed, "or by vessel between places in Canada." I think there is no doubt about that; but the sentence continues, "or from a place in Canada and return thereto." That, it seems to me, is a definite attempt to tax travel in a foreign country. With respect to international ferries, I do not think there is any doubt that all a proprietor company would have to do, provided their charge is not more than $1 return, would be to change their tariff to make it fifty cents one way,

and thus evade the tax. To my mind this tax on international ferries is a very bad one. If there is one thing more than another which we desire, it is to have United States visitors in this country leave United States funds here, and it would seem only natural that, the cheaper the fare, the more likely they are to come. I suggest that if we refrained from taxing the international ferries, the benefits to Canada would more than make up for the loss of the few dollars represented by this tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid I do not understand the hon. gentleman's difficulty. He is interested in the tourist traffic, is he not? The point is this: I do not believe there is any jurisdiction in this parliament to tax people for travelling in another country; and that is exactly what the minister is trying to do.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think there is any question about jurisdiction. Certainly, if a traveller buys a return ticket in Canada, we can tax him on that purchase.

Does the minister mean that, if you buy a ticket from, shall we say, Toronto to New York, you are taxed ten per cent on the journey in Canada, from Toronto to Niagara and from Niagara back to Toronto; or are you taxed on the journey from Niagara to New York and from New York back to Niagara?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I was talking merely about vessel transportation. That is what the hon. gentleman who spoke last was discussing. The resolution is quite clear on that, that the fare between points in Canada is taxable; the return fare from a point in Canada abroad and back, by vessel, is taxable.
And by train.
If a man purchases a return ticket from Ottawa to New York he would have to pay ten per cent on the full cost of the ticket, would he not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: According to the resolution he is taxable on the fare. If he buys a ticket from here to some point in the United States, he is taxable on that whole fare.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: He is taxable on the transaction of the purchase of the ticket, whether he travels or not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

I wish to lodge a protest against this tax on gasoline. It will cause a great hardship to many producers in western Canada. I am thinking of some refineries that have started up recently, particularly in Saskatchewan, with consumers behind them. In Saskatchewan the horse has practically disappeared; work on the farm is done with the tractor. Especially at this time when we expect the farmers to reduce their seeded acreage and do more summer-fallowing, to impose this tax is a hardship. I suggest that the minister consider cutting it down to not more than one cent.

I urge that this tax be rebated on gasoline used for agricultural purposes. Under existing conditions in western Canada, it is inevitable that present standards of farm operation cannot be maintained. There is no need to say much about the intolerable situation of agriculture throughout Canada in these times.
I have here a few figures relating to the province from which I come. The farmers of Manitoba used last year for strictly agricultural purposes 6,846,705 gallons of gasoline. Three cents a gallon on this would amount
to $205,401.15, comparable in value with 400,000 bushels of wheat or 760,745 pounds of butter fat at to-day's prices.

The Minister of Agriculture, who, I believe, is also a member of the treasury board, should at this time use his influence with the Minister of Finance to see that this tax is rebated on gasoline used for agricultural purposes.

It seems to me that

Once before I mentioned in the house that I had read in a trade magazine an authoritative article, reprinted from another periodical, to the effect that soap advertisers, for example, are spending in the United States $30,000,000 a year for radio time, exclusive of the script and the voices. I do not know what they spend in Canada. It seems to me that these are sources of revenue which could be taxed and relieve the government of the necessity for taxes of this description, which work a hardship on a depressed industry. The same thing applies, of course, to other forms of advertising. I am not singling out soap particularly. Occasionally I hear on the radio advertisers urging people to buy war savings certificates, and in the next breath they tell them that if they will bring their old knives and forks to a firm in Ottawa, that will be taken as a down payment on new tableware, which can be paid for over an extended period of time. That kind of thing is ridiculous, when we are urging people to give all the money they can for our war effort.
In my opinion the government could raise a substantial sum by imposing greater taxation on firms that are obviously making far more money than is necessary for them to operate their business, and are spending it on advertising such as I have mentioned, soap and so forth, and then giving away money, paying their radio listeners to listen to their programmes. This is a source of taxation that might well be investigated, instead of having a tax like this on gasoline used by agricultural producers.
I am not objecting at all to a federal tax at this time on gasoline used in private automobiles for pleasure purposes. Those of us who object are objecting, I believe, to another imposition on a depressed industry.
Since I do not like to suggest the elimination of a tax at this time without suggesting some alternative, I suggest that some of these other avenues of taxation be explored and that this tax be eliminated so far as the agricultural and fishing industries are concerned.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I think it was generally expected throughout this country, in the consideration not only of this budget but of the last one, that some attention would be given by the ministry to the

question of imposing a federal tax on gasoline. I do not think there has been any universal outcry against the principle of this tax, and I do not intend to make any attack on the principle of the tax to-night.
There are, however, certain inequities with respect to it that I think should be pointed out. Hon. gentlemen to my left, and some hon. members immediately surrounding me, have pointed out that a tax on gasoline without any provision for a refund will bear harshly on the agricultural industry, and I am impressed by what they have said in that regard. I am also aware of the fact that another class in this country, whose plight I think on the whole is far worse than that of the agriculturists

I refer to the fishermen along our coasts-have been given no consideration whatever. When I was a boy I lived on the coast. There was no such thing as an internal combustion engine, and we made our passage by the use of the strong spruce oar and the elbow-grease in our arms. That situation has been entirely revolutionized; to-day the gasoline engine is an absolute necessity for the fisherman. If he were obtaining a fair and reasonable return for his labour and the capital he has to invest in his vocation, I am certain he would not object at all to the payment of this tax. The fact is, however, that the ordinary fisherman on our Atlantic coast, at all events, is not only not getting a fair return for his labour or on his capital investment, but is not getting anything like a living wage. I hope the war has brought him some relief, but I doubt it; export markets, which were bad enough before the war, have been closed.
I solicit from the minister consideration on behalf of the fishermen on our Atlantic coast. That goes also for the fishermen on other coasts, although I have no intimate knowledge of their position. I know that the fishermen on the bay of Fundy and particularly the fishermen on Passamaquoddy bay have had ten lean and hungry years. Many of them have not been able to keep body and soul together; many have been unable to renew their equipment. We need only review what has been done by the government in days gone by, in attempts to relieve the plight of the fishermen, to realize their position, and I think the minister should reconsider applying this tax to everyone and should give some consideration to the fishermen of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Quebec and Prince Edward Island. I am making a special plea for them, not that other fishermen may not have the

Special War Revenue Act
same need but because I know more about the condition of the fishermen in the provinces I have mentioned.
I realize that there are difficulties with respect to this question of drawbacks. I know that in days gone by there have been frauds perpetrated on the provincial governments, all of which have this provision. It is very difficult to detect and convict in such cases. I venture to suggest that not one offence in ten is actually detected and the person convicted, but that does not mean that the class as a whole are dishonest. Far from it. There are crooks in every trade, but notwithstanding all that, I ask the minister to give some consideration to the farmers and the fishermen with respect to drawbacks.
I should also like to point out to this committee that with the imposition of this tax we in the maritime provinces are being taxed on gasoline more than any other people in the world. Is it realized generally that in the three maritime provinces we have had a tax of ten cents a gallon on gasoline for several years past?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think that is right. There are some inequalities in this tax, and it would be pretty hard to apply it all along the line I suppose it could be done; it could be applied to fuel oil, to distillate and so forth, but I doubt whether that would be in accord with the wishes of the house or of the people. Practically speaking, it is- impossible to impose taxes without creating some discrimination. There is only one tax that is without discrimination; that is the income tax. If we could limit ourselves to that form of taxation, we would avoid practically all discrimination, but the moment we go into taxation of this kind, some discrimination is bound to result.
I think the minister will find that if fuel oil for diesel engines is not taxed, some of the companies now using gasoline will switch to the use of fuel oil in order to meet the competition.

A few days ago two men were walking down Wellington street, near this building. One of them suddenly stopped and said, "I smell something burning." His companion turned round and replied, "That is Canada speeding up her war effort, with the brake on." If we consider the treatment that has been given agriculture during the last five or six years, or even longer, I think it will be agreed that the brake has been applied so far as agriculture is concerned. This latest imposition, this three-cent tax on gasoline used for farm purposes, will tighten up that brake at least one more notch-and, as somebody says, it smells. I do not disagree with that. Time after time in this house we have pointed out the condition of agriculture. On various occasions the Minister of Agriculture has admitted that we have sold at far less than the cost of production. If we were getting what we are entitled to at the present time, we would be getting $1.35 for our wheat, but we are getting 70 cents. I ask: Is it any wonder that man smelled something burning?
The position of the industrialist was very well stated a few moments ago by the hon
Special War Revenue Act

member for Waterloo South when he said: "What is the use of having a war, if we cannot spend?" That, apparently, is the position of industry to-day, and industry is apparently controlling the government, because if somebody does not spend, another gang cannot make profits. I say that the gang is profiteering at the expense of agriculture.
What gang?
The gang of profiteers. Perhaps they are some of your friends, too.
Who are they?

I see one of them with his hand on his head, I believe. If the Minister of Finance could go all through Canada-and I am not speaking of western Canada alone, because I do not believe he will have to go far from Ottawa-listen to the cries of undernourished children, and the moaning of some of the mothers of those children, and look into the asylums where the fathers have been driven, because they are not able to get a living for their families, I believe some of the inequalities would be done away with.
Social credit.
I wish that log bump would be quiet once in a while-'bump on a log, I mean.
You were right the first time.

Some people cannot make a speech, or do anything for their constituents; and they will not let anybody else talk for their constituents. I wish they would keep quiet, and let some of us speak, while those fellows are too busy keeping their chairs warm.
I believe the government realizes full well the condition of agriculture. We are asked to do certain things; we are asked to make equality of sacrifice, and in that way to maintain Canadian unity. I ask the Minister of Finance if he thinks, in all fairness to agriculture, we are getting the deal to which we are entitled, when this three-cent tax is imposed. It may be argued that it is impossible to free agriculture of that tax. It has, however, been pointed out in this debate that two provinces, namely, Saskatchewan and Alberta, have coloured gasoline for agricultural purposes. When gasoline is exempted from taxation in those two provinces, I believe the other provinces might very well adopt the same method, whereby their gasoline for agricultural purposes could easily be identified. There is no argument whatever, so far as that is concerned.
I believe I should put in a word for the fishermen, too. We have heard on different occasions that they are suffering, and I have
fMr. Fair.]
no doubt about that at all. I have never been to the east or west coasts, because I have been too busy trying to pay my way, farming. I have not had the price to make those trips. But we have heard from hon. members representing the fishermen that those fishermen are in a terrible plight.
I was surprised to hear the leader of the opposition speak for them, because I think in the past he and his party should have done something worth while to ease the conditions of those people.
They did.

I heard a lawyer from down Halifax way say one time that when he was going through a cemetery he saw a headstone with a single name on it. At the foot of the headstone was the inscription, "Here lies an honest man and a lawyer." He said, "Be jabers, what is the other fellow's name?" He thought there were two buried, whereas there was actually only one.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Give us something new.
The first time we have ever heard thatl

I am not going to say much more. I have said before that the government realizes full well , the condition of agriculture. I am asking the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Agriculture and all their colleagues to get together to work out some solution whereby gasoline for farm production will be exempted from the tax.

In so far as this tax on gasoline is a tax on pleasure, I am not opposed to it. I believe that during war time any expenditure for pleasure travel must be taxed, if the government is going to raise money to carry on the war. In so far, however, as this gasoline tax constitutes a tax upon production, a tax upon primary producers, and has the effect of increasing their cost of production-which, in many instances, they are not now receiving-it is most unfair, and I protest against it.
I cannot speak with any authority for the fishermen, but most of us who live on the prairies know the situation with regard to wheat farmers. The situation for the last few years has been this: The decline in the price of wheat has meant that the farmers have been more and more forced into tractor farming. When this government came into power there was a guaranteed minimum price of 87^ cents, basis Fort William. That was dropped to eighty cents, and in 1938 it was dropped to sixty cents. It was raised to seventy cents only because of the protests which came from all over western Canada.

The Minister of Agriculture made his famous speech in which he spoke of wheat being produced for from thirty cents to forty cents a bushel, having in mind himself the fact that the wheat which could be produced at a figure like that was wheat which was produced on a mechanized farm. For the last two years we have had a price basis of -seventy cents, basis Fort William, and that meant forty-nine or fifty cents to the farmer. The result was that the only man who could possibly produce was the man who went into tractor farming. Then, for the past few years those tractors have been more and more of the high compression variety, using high-grade fuel.
Then came the war. It has not only not given any increase in prices of the products the farmers have to sell, but has meant an increase in their cost of production. The price of farm machinery has gone up. Almost everything the farmer has to buy has risen in price. Under this legislation, the price of his fuel is going to go up. Then, to add just one thing more, the Minister of Agriculture has brought in legislation to provide for a wheat acreage reduction bonus. That, combined with the legislation of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, is going to restrict farmers to the sale of about forty-eight per cent of the wheat they sold last year. They are going to be asked to summer-fallow as much as possible of the land they are taking out of wheat. If that land is going to be summer-fallowed, then in a great many instances it will be summer-fallowed most economically by the tractor farmers. The cost of summer-fallowing will be increased materially by this tax of three cents a gallon.
It is bad enough to say to the farmer. "You will not be able to sell as much wheat as you sold last year." It is bad enough to say, "You must go out and summer-fallow your land in order to get $4 an acre." But it is the last straw on the already shaky camel's back to say, "You are now to increase your cost of summer-fallowing and the general cost of your farming operations by having to pay three cents a gallon as tax on your fuel."
Has any consideration been given by the government to the possibility of giving a rebate on all gasoline purchased by primary producers for the purpose of carrying on farming and fishing operations? The principle is sound. It has been accepted in several provinces. Various techniques have been used, and I am not prepared to argue that one is better than another. That is the government's problem. But it has been worked out in other provinces in various ways, and
they have found it is not impossible to give a rebate to the primary producers for fuel used for all productive purposes. There is no reason why this government cannot do the same thing. It could, if it wished, arrange that farmers should buy their fuel for tractors in bulk quantities. It could be arranged that the fuel would be bought in barrels. Sworn statements could be made, and rebates could be given at the end of the year. Some provinces do that. Other provinces have a specially coloured gasoline. In Saskatchewan the number of convictions has not been high. People have tried to use this coloured gasoline for pleasure purposes, but they have been haled into court and punished. I think in the main the primary producing class realizes that in giving them a rebate on gasoline the government is doing something for them to which they have a right, but if they want to enjoy that privilege they must play the game. The great mass of the people have played the game.
I do not think the government would have any difficulty in working out a technique whereby a rebate could be paid to the farmers and fishermen on the gasoline used in their farming and fishing operations. I cannot think of anything that will do more to kill the morale of the wheat farmer than the announcement, which has been received by him with dismay and astonishment, of the government's legislation and acreage bonus plan. The picture will be completed if we have to go west and tell them that the fuel used in their farming operations will cost them three cents a gallon more than it did last year. Has consideration been given to the payment of a rebate on gasoline used for farming operations? What is the estimated loss of revenue to the treasury if such a rebate were paid? Will the government consider including this in the legislation when it is brought down?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not remember ever having given more consideration to any one matter since I have been minister than I have given to this question of a rebate of this gasoline tax. Long weary hours were spent by myself with the officials in trying to devise some system of refunds which would not bring the government of Canada into disrepute with the people. The more the matter was studied, the more the operation of provincial systems of refunds was examined into, the more it became apparent that unless we desired to embark upon a system which would bring about wholesale evasion in all parts of the country, we had better keep away from rebates or refunds.

What about using coloured gas? That would not require a refund.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, yes.
A man buys the coloured gas for agricultural purposes, and he does not pay a tax. If that gas is found in his car being used for pleasure purposes, he is prosecuted.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That was all gone into. I talked to representatives of the provinces and to members of the governments of the provinces where the rebate or refund system was in effect. Those provinces consider that their system is better than the coloured gas system. I am told that in one of the provinces where the coloured gas system is in effect, they have from 100 to 200 prosecutions a month and require a large number of inspectors.
Which province is that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not wish to say.
There are only two.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. member can make his choice because I am not going to make any accusation against either of those provinces. It is within the knowledge of everyone, especially the members of the provincial administrations, that it is impossible to operate a system whereby a large amount of tax-free gas as well as a large amount of taxed gas are used by the public without having wholesale evasions. The leader of the opposition frankly admitted that in a speech which he made. Members of this administration who have had experience in provincial administrations have told us that it would never do for the dominion government, so far away from so much of the country as it is, to be trying to check upon the use of tax-free gasoline. The people should be conscientious about these matters, but many of them are not.
If the government of Canada is to maintain its reputation, it must not embark upon such a policy. One of the premiers of the provinces went so far as to say that if the government went into this system of rebates or refunds of the gasoline tax, it would defeat them. Not that that is the supreme consideration, but he meant that it would defeat them because they would deserve to be defeated on account of the abuses which would naturally arise in all parts of the country. We must have some regard for practicability; we must have some regard for the respect which the people of Canada ought to have
TMr. Ilsley.]
and ought to maintain toward the government of this country, and its methods of taxing and administering taxes. It is quite easy to say that this or that should be taxed, but very often the reason why a tax which would be ideal if it could be administered is not imposed is the widespread abuses which would occur.
We gave consideration to imposing a much higher tax upon gasoline and providing refunds, not only for farmers and fishermen but also for tourists. We did not want the tourists who come to this country to be paying this gasoline tax. The people whom we would like to have pay this tax are those who are using gasoline for pleasure purposes. If the tax could be confined to them, I would be disposed to consider a much higher tax. It is in the interests of the country to discourage the heavy importations of crude oil and petroleum products which are refined to be used for pleasure purposes. I am convinced, however, that there is only one way in which this government can administer the gasoline tax in a satisfactory manner, and that is by collecting it from the refineries. Thus we get the tax on all the gasoline, whether it is used for commercial or pleasure purposes, by tourists, by farmers, by fishermen or by any one else. That is why we put on a three cent tax when everyone expected a five cent tax. We felt that we would just have to ask the farming and fishing populations of this country, as well as the tourists who come here, to bear this moderate additional burden.
I knew that there would be a debate like this. I knew that certain members would rise in their places to speak on behalf of the fishermen; I knew that others would want to speak on behalf of the farmers, while perhaps others would be pointing out the injury which might be done to the tourist business. I do not think there is much in that because I understand that the United States government is proposing a tax of 24 cents a gallon. That would be equivalent to our tax of three cents a gallon when the difference between the United States and the Canadian gallon is considered. Much as I should have liked to avoid any tax upon agriculturists or fishermen, or, for that matter, upon the commercial use of gasoline, after giving the matter the most extended consideration I was unable to come to the conclusion that I would be justified in bringing in a measure which would have involved a non-administrable system of rebates or refunds, or taxation only on gasoline of some colour.

The gasoline tax is good in another way. The consumption of gasoline, as we all know, is increasing tremendously. I do not think this tax is going to be a tremendous hardship. After all, every single one of us is in the front line, and we must all be prepared to shoulder a little bit more of the burden.

Has any provincial
government offered to collect this gasoline tax on the consideration that the tax be rebated to agriculturists? Would it not be possible, by cooperation, for the provincial governments to handle the collection of the tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We fully considered whether we should adopt the refund system in the provinces. We then would have had a checker-14873-190
board policy, with one set of people getting refunds in one province and a slightly different set of people getting refunds in another province. It would be a vicious principle to introduce into dominion legislation.
The hon. gentleman asked, did any province offer to collect the tax? I would not go so far as to say that any province offered, but a minister in one provincial government did go so far as to ask me if I had considered that. I did consider it, but not favourably.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It having been established with some definiteness that the minister is not disposed to yield to the representations made to him, the position of agriculturists and fishermen having been championed valiantly, I turn to another aspect. What method does the minister propose with respect to the collection of this revenue? I heard him say a moment ago that he intended to have the tax paid by the refineries. What about the importing companies? May I point out to him that all the provinces have arrangements with the distributors whereby they deduct the tax from the retailers, who in turn charge the tax to their customers. That, in my view, is wholly unconstitutional, but that is the method adopted as a matter of convenience. The point has never been raised in the courts. I thought I had in my portfolio a statement of the cost to the various provinces of the collection and remission of this tax by that'method. I know it runs into a good many thousands of dollars, and I warn the minister that he should make better arrangements than some of the provinces have made because some people are getting a substantial compensation-I shall not say rake-off-for the collection and remission of this tax. I am sorry I have not the data under my hand, but I have no doubt it is available to the department. If the minister has the information at hand, it might be revealing to the committee to know just what the figures are. I know that such a statement has been compiled.
Has the minister or the government ever given consideration to the nationalization of the oil business in Canada? That is a big problem, and I do not wish to start a discussion of it to-night except to say that other countries have nationalized universally consumed products, and that the time may come when we shall have to give consideration to that in this country. If it could be done here, it would yield huge Sums of money to the federal treasury without adding one cent to the cost to the consumer. I suppose I am flirting with a tremendously big problem, and
