the government, of course, will not give consideration to it now. I suggest, however, to the minister that it is worthy of consideration if this war lasts long enough.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think I shall deal with the last part of my hon. friend's remarks because, as he says, that is a pretty big problem. As to compensation to the refiners for collecting the tax, that question does not arise because this is a tax upon the refiners. This is not a tax upon the consumer or upon the purchasers from the refiners as it is in the provinces. The provinces can impose only direct taxation, but there is no such constitutional limitation upon the powers of the dominion parliament, and we therefore simply place the tax at the source and pay no compensation to anybody. In that respect the tax is administered like the sales tax.
In the case of importations the tax will be collected from the importer. That is provided for in the resolution.

The minister seems to be a little bit worried over two aspects of this gasoline tax. First, there is the desire to conserve foreign exchange, and he is no doubt on sound ground in bringing this tax forward for that purpose. If, however, it is just a question of conserving foreign exchange, there are other fields which would be much more productive in that respect. I have in mind coal. We could save a tremendous amount of foreign exchange if we were to use a little more Canadian coal, and we might then not need this tax on gasoline.
Second, I can visualize that, before very long, we may be in danger of a shortage of gasoline. Speaking three years ago on this subject of oil and gasoline and the possibility of an invasion of the oil-producing countries of Asia like Iran and Iraq, I suggested, before the war broke out, that one of the most essential things to Canada was the development of the oil fields of Alberta. I pointed out three years ago that in Alberta we had the greatest potential oil fields of the whole British empire, and I urged that every means available be adopted to develop our oil industry. I suggested at that time-and it is not yet too late to draw the matter to the government's attention again-that a pipeline should be built from Alberta to British Columbia. We have large reserves of oil in the northern part of the tar sands, and while production may be expensive, I do not think the cost of refining the oil should be considered in view of the grave danger of the British fleet becoming in dire need of oil. fVr. R. B. Hanson.]
I would go farther than that. If the minister is at all alarmed as to a possible shortage of gasoline, now would be an opportune time to ration it. Such a ' course, I believe, would be much more practicable than to impose a tax, unless, of course, the minister has in mind purely a means of raising revenue, and I take it that that is not his only reason for imposing this tax.
It must be remembered that some industries would be affected more than others by this tax. I believe I am correct in saying that when, a couple of years ago, we placed an eight per cent tax on electricity, an exemption was given in respect of power used for industrial purposes. Is that right?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

If, then, industries were exempted from the tax on electricity in order to keep down their costs of production, what logical reason is there why the agricultural industry and, if you will, the fishing industry, should not be exempted on exactly the same ground? If we are going to establish any sort of equality of sacrifice, it is certainly not a square deal to say to agriculture, as the Minister of Agriculture said not long ago in this chamber, that ninety cents a bushel at Fort William was a fair and reasonable price for wheat, after which the price was reduced to seventy cents, which means an average of about fifty cents to the Alberta and Saskatchewan farmers, and now we are to reduce their returns still further. It seems to me that agriculture will be very much dissatisfied. I know of nothing in the form of a tax which would cause more widespread concern than the imposition of a tax of three cents a gallon on gasoline used for agricultural purposes. I am in agreement with other hon. members, however, that a gasoline tax would be less objectionable if it were not applied to gasoline used for agricultural purposes.
The minister suggests that it would be difficult to administer an exemption of this kind. I believe that that difficulty could be easily overcome if the assistance of the provinces were asked in this regard. The minister mentioned a few moments ago that hundreds of prosecutions were taking place in certain provinces because of the rebate on gasoline for farming purposes. I know of only two provinces, namely, Saskatchewan and Alberta, in which a rebate is in operation. Alberta adopted it only a very short time ago; so the only province in which prosecutions can be taking place is, apparently, Saskatchewan; and in that event I shall let the representatives of Saskatchewan speak for that province, but I am quite convinced

Special War Revenue Act
that in Alberta the system will work out very satisfactorily, much better indeed than the old form of rebate did.
What is the system?

A purple gas, royal purple, is used for this purpose in Alberta. There is no possible chance of its being used for commercial purposes.
One hon. member opposite made an excellent suggestion in advocating a tax on diesel fuel. I am not proposing a tax on that fuel when used for agricultural purposes; but I think his point was well made that in some commercial businesses, as well as in agriculture, certain types of engines use diesel fuel, the consequence being that, for instance, the farmer running a large diesel tractor has no gasoline tax to pay, while his neighbour who operates a gasoline engine is taxed on the fuel he uses. It is ridiculous to suggest that their costs of production are equal. Or take the case of the commercial men who are engaged in trucking. One uses a diesel truck and the other a gasoline truck; they are competing in exactly the same field, yet one is taxed and the other is not. To me that does not seem fair, and I do not believe the minister can convince himself that it is. It would be much more satisfactory to adopt the principle of taxing all fuel, allowing a rebate on that portion which is used for agricultural purposes.
Comparing the treatment of industries which are allowed a rebate on their electrical power, with that accorded to the farmers and the fishermen, I do not believe that any sane person can argue that it is either fair or logical or equitable. Here we have an industry which is trying its utmost to live up to the government's expectations. As the Minister of Agriculture says, it is producing at a loss. He says, "We do not expect them to make a profit". Well, they are not asking for a profit. But surely, when they are producing at a loss, we should not add insult to injury by yet further increasing their costs of production. Consider, too, that the purchase of gasoline by farmers is a direct cash outlay. When they go to these big oil companies, such as the Imperial Oil, does anyone suppose that they can get gasoline until fall on credit? They certainly cannot; the very first thing one sees on an agent's door is the notice, "terms strictly cash". Yet the farmer is not permitted even to sell his grain, and under a new order he cannot exchange his wheat for his neighbour's coarse grain or anything else. Where is he going to get money for his summer-fallow?
From the government.
He is not a lawyer; he is a farmer. We are speaking of farmers.
If he is a farmer, why does he not try horses again?
Where is the profit in horses?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
Do we want to go back to the old ox-stage of farming?
Horses are much better.

When we think of the conditions under which farmers are labouring, and the sacrifices they are making in this war, this tax certainly is not a fair proposition. We are going out on a victory loan campaign. We are going to visit all these farmers. I have a great deal of sympathy with the fellow who goes to the first farmer and says to him, "Listen, brother, the government wants you to give some more in the victory loans", and at the same time the tax collector comes around and takes another three cents on each gallon of gas the farmer uses. I certainly have no desire to go out under conditions like that. Here is a man who is producing now at a loss, who is trying his best to subscribe to the war loans, who is asked to contribute to the salvage campaign, and is doing it all willingly. Yet now the government comes along, and increases, absolutely unnecessarily, the tax on gasoline used for agricultural purposes. It is nothing short of a crime. The government should consider seriously the advisability of amending its legislation so as to rebate to the farmer the tax on gasoline used for agricultural purposes.
I should like to have an opportunity of saying a word to the hon. member who has just spoken.

The cities and urban
centres will pay four-fifths of this tax, but they seem to have very little voice in this house, since we have to listen to others whom the tax will affect but little. This three cents a gallon tax on gasoline manufactured or produced in Canada or imported will be a heavy burden on the industrial workers of the cities and towns who pay the bulk of this form of taxation in order to go to and from their work. This gasoline tax started in the early days of the motor car. The main municipalities in Ontario went to the Ontario government and said they had to provide pavements, roads, police protection, fire protection, curbs, and protect and locate these
Special War Revenue Act

tanks and take care of them and it cost a lot of money for inspection, so they asked the government to give them taxation powers. The government refused, but when the cities discovered the tax, the province appropriated it. What did the provincial government do? They did just like the dominion. The moment a municipality finds a source of taxation other than real estate, the province grabs it. Then, when the municipalities ask for half of it back, the province refuses, and now the federal power seizes the tax and duplicates it, without giving any service.
It would be better if the minister were not so fond of his own hobby of asking questions himself, because the more questions he asks, the more discussion he promotes in this house as he cross-examines and asks questions and supplies answers. The minister is exercising most unfairly the Pooh-Bah powers he has to-day. It was he who wanted to have the Sirois report adopted. He has taken the thunder and used it unfairly to the injury of municipal institutions. If the dominion is going to impose this form of taxation, the dominion should at least give part of it back to the municipalities, who give the services, roads and gasoline protection. The dominion does not render any services in return, but impounds the tax. In the riding of the hon. member next to me, Cumberland, Nova Scotia, I think the provincial tax is about ten cents, and this addition will make thirteen cents a gallon, a practically prohibitive tax, that cannot be passed on and will cause heavy lack of consumption. In other words, to pay a tax of thirteen cents is about three times what it used to cost to produce and buy gasoline. This system, in this budget, has upset the whole taxation principle; where is it going to end? It simply means that the municipalities will starve because the minister will not give them back any part of the proceeds; he will not do it, and the provinces will not do it. They starve municipal institutions and ruin them. Eighty per cent of this form of taxation is paid by the two central industrial provinces. I ask the minister to consider where this form of taxation is going to land the provinces and the municipalities. It is going to force them into bankruptcy under socialism in our time. That is what they are heading for.
As I said when the minister introduced his budget, many of the resolutions relate to what they do in England and Washington. But in England they have no provinces, and in Washington they have a different system. A tax like this is unjust, unfair and inequitable, sounds the death knell of our system of taxation, will lead to the bankruptcy of the

provinces and municipalities, is in restraint of trade and commerce, and causes disunity, waste and duplication. The result will be that the government will get less money if this continues, with drastic reduction in consumption. Under the minister's Pooh-Bah powers he will be putting a further direct tax not only on real estate but, in time, on the very air that we breathe in this chamber.

I should like to ask a
question. Is this tax not most just?
No.

Farmer members were hitting the man with the big farm who raises thousands of bushels of wheat. This tax does not touch the man who works his farm with a team. A man who can afford to buy a tractor has a right to pay the tax and save the man with the team. I do not care whether a man comes from Saskatchewan or anywhere else, if he can buy four or five tractors he can under-sell the man who works his farm with a team. Therefore I say that this tax is fair and just because it is a tax on the man at the top who has the money.

I join with the leader of the opposition and other hon. members who have made a plea to the minister to rebate this tax to farmers and fishermen. I was in the Nova Scotia legislature when the gasoline tax was first put into effect, and we had some misgivings with respect to the rebate, but wre were able to work it out so that I believe there was not any, or very little, injustice practised by the farmers and fishermen. I do not agree with the minister that there is dishonesty among the great bulk of farmers and fishermen who would receive the rebate of this tax. There is no class of people in Canada more entitled to special consideration than the farmers of eastern Canada. They above all others are the neglected class; they are having great difficulty in carrying on their operations. That applies to the farmers of eastern Canada and to the fishermen on the Atlantic coast, including the lobster fishermen whom the government has had to assist in marketing their catch at a comparatively low price. This additional tax on the lobster fishermen will mean a great burden to them.
It is also a real burden on the farmers in eastern Canada to pay an extra tax on the gasoline used in their motor vehicles. We have in Nova Scotia some 15,000 to 16,000 miles of highway, of which only about 1,000 miles are paved. That leaves about 15,000 miles of mud and earth roads on which the farmer has to operate his car. Very few farmers can carry on their operations to-day

Special War Revenue Act
without a motor car, even though it is a second-hand car and not economical as regards consumption of gasoline. Most of the farms are on these mud, earth and gravel roads. Therefore, from that point of view the farmer is entitled to special consideration.
Again I say that the system we have in effect in Nova Scotia for giving rebates to the farmers has worked veiy well, and in my experience the instances are rare where there has been dishonesty on the part of farmers or fishermen.
Therefore I join with the leader of the opposition and hon. members representing agricultural sections and ask the minister to give further consideration to granting rebate or exemption to the farmers and fishermen in eastern Canada, in view of their dire need.

I do not agree with the case the minister has made for refusing to grant exemption from this tax on gasoline used for farming and fishing operations. What reason has the minister given? Is it that he needs the revenue? He has not said so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, I do.

Nor has the minister said he cannot find that revenue in some other way. In fact, the minister has agreed in principle that, if possible, this tax should not be placed on people who are using gasoline in production. The minister says he examined that aspect of the matter, and that, if possible, that would have been provided for.
Last year, in the first war budget, when an exemption was given to industrial concerns using electricity, the minister recognized that the principle of taxing production, and consequently increasing the cost of production, was unsound, and that it was better to examine the advisability of giving exemptions wherever it was possible to do so. The minister's only reason, then, for refusing to exempt from this tax gasoline used in farming and fishing operations is the administrative difficulties. The minister's statement is a reflection upon a great section of the people of Canada as well as upon the provinces. He tells us that there would be wholesale evasions of this tax, that there would be, on a large scale, abuse of the exemption. He says further that all the provinces which are trying to carry on a system of rebates warned him that this was the last thing to be done, and that one of the provinces using coloured gasoline had something like two hundred cases of evasion a month. The only province that has been using coloured gasoline for any length of
time, so far as I know, is Saskatchewan, and certainly the information which comes to me from policemen and others in judicial capacities would not lead me to believe that figure to be correct.
The minister's statement is a reflection on the provinces. If they are finding widespread abuses of this exemption, why do they continue it? If they are finding that people are using, for pleasure purposes, gasoline allegedly bought for farming and fishing operations, they should discontinue that exemption, but they have not done so. Not a single province has withdrawn that exemption, and so it would not appear that this argument is borne out by the practice in the various provinces.
But, the minister says, the federal government is further removed, and it would be much more difficult to administer this exemption. That is a point to be considered, but there is no reason why it could not be operated in conjunction with the provinces. The refineries could sell taxable gasoline, and tax-free gasoline which would be especially coloured. The federal government could easily arrange with the provincial governments, through their provincial police or the mounted police, that any person picked up and found using tax-free gasoline in his automobile would be charged, not only by the provincial government but also by the federal government, with evasion of the tax. The two governments could cooperate in bringing charges against any person who evaded the tax, and any person abusing the privilege would be charged with violating not only the provincial statute but the federal statute as well.
I know the minister will say, "Oh, it is easy for opposition members to rise in their places and tell me how this can be done," but I say to the minister that this is the most amazing thing I have ever heard. Here we have a minister of the crown saying that the principle is sound; that the producers have a right to be exempted from this tax, but that they must pay the tax because he considers the administrative difficulties to be insurmountable. That is an unsound principle; I believe it is a lame excuse. I do not think the farming population will take it very kindly if they have a tax placed upon them which the minister cannot justify except by the fact that some of them may cheat.

I am well aware that no words of mine will affect the passing of this resolution; that is, that they will have no direct effect, but it may be proper that someone from British Columbia should voice the feelings of the fishermen and farmers of that province. I do not, of course, intend any
Special War Revenue Act

reflection on the other members from British Columbia, some of whom are attending committees that are sitting at the moment.
I would point out to the minister that for days we have been sitting here passing taxes on luxuries, and that we have yet to pass taxes on playing cards, wines, cigarette papers and so forth. This is not a tax on a luxury; it is a tax on a working tool, part of the machinery of the farmer and fisherman. The comment has been made that any exemption would be difficult to enforce, but so far as my knowledge goes, we have had no particular trouble in that regard in British Columbia. At one time I was agent for an oil company. The gasoline we sold farmers and fishermen was a pretty pink in colour, like a lady's blouse. If a man was caught driving a car that had pink gasoline in its tank, he had to pay a heavy fine. His tank would hold only about ten gallons of gasoline. The man who bootlegged the gasoline to him would have to make something out of it, so the man would not save more than twenty-five cents at the most, while his fine would amount to perhaps $10. Therefore it would not pay him to go into that business, nor would it pay the farmer or fisherman to go into the bootlegging of gasoline, and consequently we did not have very much trouble so far as I can recall.
I would point out that the fishermen have to use gasoline in order to carry on their business. A fishing boat must travel at a very slow speed, and anyone who drives a car knows that if it is driven at either a very high or a very low speed it uses a great deal of gasoline. These fishing boats, which have to be kept moving at a very slow speed, are costly to operate because of their high gasoline consumption. If a farmer ploughs all day, he can at least look over his field at the end of the day and see the result of his labours. The fisherman, however, can work all night and burn his gasoline, and in the morning have perhaps only one miserable fish. I have seen a fisherman come in with one fish, and even the fish itself looked sort of ashamed. One of the first parables in the Bible tells of divine providence taking compassion on men who had been fishing all night and caught, nothing. In those days, however, they lost only their labour. To-day the fisherman loses his labour and, in addition, the cash he has paid for gasoline, which is quite considerable.
I know one thing that will happen on the west coast as a result of this increased tax. Smuggling will be given a tremendous impetus, and perhaps I personally might suggest it to some of my fishermen friends out there. All they have to do is to send a boat over to Seattle to get gasoline and then meet the boat on the high seas, outside the three mile

limit, where the gasoline can be transferred to the fishing boats. If a fisherman comes in with three or four gallons in his tank, who is going to proceed against him for that? Certainly there will be a temptation to do that sort of thing. The other day, in connection with the tax on beer or malt or something similar, the minister said it would lead to the operation of illicit stills, and the same principle will apply in this instance.
The fisherman has a hard time of it. The leader of the opposition has spoken about conditions on the east coast, and the situation in the west is similar. The fisherman needs all the aid he can obtain. During the last ten days I have heard a number of these items discussed. I have seen members rise in their places and wax vociferous over the injustice or hardship that would be imposed by the particular item to which they objected, but not one of them appeared to have the intestinal fortitude to put it to a vote. I suppose to-night at least two dozen hon. members have spoken against this tax. I wonder how many of them would vote against it? They need not be afraid. It will not /.efeat the government; it will not be a vote of want of confidence, and the vote will not be recorded. Why not rise in your place and show what you think about it? It will not make any difference to the tax; it will still be imposed; but at least it may impress upon the government the fact that a great many people object to this tax, and that might be all to the good when these matters are being considered next session. I invite those who oppose the tax to show their courage. As the French say, "Oh! j'ai du courage"; have the courage of your convictions and vote against this tax.

It is difficult not to agree with much of what has been said by the hon. gentleman who has just spoken. We should, however, not forget the task of the Minister of Finance, particularly at this time. Many of the hon. members who have opposed this tax also have opposed several of the other proposals that have been put forward by the minister. Obviously, if we are to carry on the war, money must be found. Oppressive as some of these taxes are, they will simply have to be met. While I do not oppose the imposition of the three-cent tax during war time by this parliament, there are certain avenues of extenuation which have not yet been explored.
The justification for the tax is that the money is needed. It is a severe tax, not simply because of the three cents we are imposing, but because the combined taxes of the federal and provincial governments make

Special War Revenue Act
the burden an oppressive one. I believe in Ontario the tax is eight cents. It is imposed by a government which asserted that it was imposed for one purpose, and one purpose alone, namely, the maintenance and the development of highways.
Did they live up to that?
No; they did not. That does not apply only to the present government in Ontario. It applies to its predecessor.
Why did you have to go back to that?
You might have left that out.
If the hon. member will try to maintain a level of discussion, with which he is not too much accustomed, I think we shall get along very well.
Politics.

At the present time at least one province has been able fortunately to show a surplus in its financial position. That province, like others at the present time, is not now engaged in further highway developments, and is keeping highway maintenance costs at a minimum. Highways are not being improved. True, gravel highways are being cared for, but the upkeep of highways in general is being kept at a minimum.
It seems to me that, having that in mind, eleven cents a gallon is a very severe tax.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
What
about thirteen cents?

Yes; in the hon. member's province it is thirteen cents. I believe such a tax is oppressive, not only on the farmers, but also on those who have to go to factories, and on others generally. A tax of eleven cents on a gallon of gasoline which sells for thirty-three cents, twenty-six cents or eighteen cents is nothing short of being oppressive.
I do not see how we can escape the imposition of the three-cent tax. The minister has made a proposal with regard to personal income tax and corporation tax. He has proposed to the provincial governments that if they vacate these two fields he will provide compensation. Obviously the analogy in this case is not complete, because the vacating of the gasoline tax field by the provinces could not provoke an offer corresponding with that which waS made in the case of personal income tax and corporation tax. But it does seem to me-and possibly the minister can give us some enlightenment on the point

that some
arrangement could be made with the provinces with regard to this particular matter. Some compensation might be arranged. It could not be a complete compensation, having in mind the disparity between the tax in the province and the proposed tax of three cents in the dominion.
The minister has heard expressions from all sides of the house as to the severity of the tax on those engaged in agriculture. He might have heard expressions quite easily from other groups on behalf of other people engaged in other occupations. Would it not be advisable, in view of the fact that the invasion by the dominion of the field of taxation now occupied by the provinces has been kept at a minimum, including only the corporation tax, succession duties and income tax-
And picture shows.

That, I suggest, is another matter. It does seem to me, however, that, having in mind the fact that we have invaded the provincial field, and having in mind their assurance of their desire to assist us at this time of crisis, the minister might well make some proposal to the provinces whereby they could vacate this field entirely, or, if not entirely, to an extent which would make the tax less burdensome than it now is.

The discussion has widened out to the land again to-night, and I should like to take issue with some of the observations which have been made by the hon. member for Weyburn, and also the hon. member for Bow River. I appreciate very much the kindliness of those members who are always endeavouring to look after the interests of the farmers. Being a farmer myself, I feel rather humiliated by the fact that when legislation comes up in this chamber they are always depicting the farmer as some sort of mendicant, who is always wanting charity.
Is this charity?
He is wanting equality.

I do not interrupt other hon.
members. When I want my soul fed up with fresh celestial fare, I like to go to church on Sundays and listen to the minister. But when I get it six days in the week-well, that is just a little bit too much.
It might have some effect.

I can appreciate a good
sermon, and it has a good effect; but some of them, I might say are not very effective.

That is quite obvious.
Special War Revenue Act

I do not wish to hurt the
feelings of hon. members, but the thing which impresses me is that very often those people who are loud in the interests of agriculture are those who do not have a foot of ground. Their shoes have never been soiled. It seems to me characteristic of some people-and I notice it so much in this chamber-to talk on matters about which they know so little.

Such as the hon. member
for Fort William.

If hon. members cannot suggest something better, in place of this tax, to raise the revenue for this countiy, they would be wise to take the suggestion of the hon. member for Fraser Valley and tax speeches. If that were done, I believe hon. members in the group opposite would not have anything left by way of sessional indemnity.
Mr. MaoNICOL:	Would the hon. member speak a little louder? He is doing fine.

I do not know whether I
should take that as a compliment, or not. Is it because the hon. member cannot hear me that he thinks I am doing fine?
The hon. member for Weyburn made the statement that the difficulty with agriculture in the west is it has reached the stage where it has been forced into mechanized tractor farming. My viewpoint is that it has been the tractors which have created the difficulty and hardship in the west.
Does the hon. member live in the west?

I am still led to the belief, in spite of the fact that I may be called old-fashioned, and that it may be said that I am still in the ox-cart days, that if many farmers had not invested so much money in mechanized farming, and had kept to the horses-and I am not saying that there is not a proper place for tractors

they would not have had some of the difficulties with which they are confronted to-day. As the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has said, very often they would have only the loss of labour. When a crop failure occurs you are faced with large expenses which you otherwise would not have had if you had kept to a smaller field of activity.
Hon. members of the Social Credit group and the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation are always condemning industry for being greedy, but I think some of the people they are championing are wanting too much. The trouble is the man who overexpanded, who went out to make a fortune and got licked in the process. The average farmer who did 
not buy a tractor until he had the money to pay for it has not suffered so much. Last year there was an increase of about forty per cent in purchases of agricultural implements in Canada. I do not think all the farmers who bought tractors were absolutely foolish. They would not have bought tractors if they had not some reason for so doing, and they must have expected to have to pay for their gasoline and any tax that might be placed upon gasoline.
I think the average farmer wants to pay his share of the taxes. He has in his veins much of that old pioneering blood which came out from the old country many years ago. He considers it is a privilege to make a contribution to society by the payment of taxes. I have not had one letter of protest from my constituency in connection with these taxes. Hon. members opposite claim they have, but I do not know why they should have, more than I.
The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) wanted to know how the farmers would be able to purchase these war bonds that are going to be put out for sale shortly. Perhaps the committee will bear with me while I draw attention to something that occurred twenty-five years ago at the time of the victory loan campaign. The population of one of the smallest townships in Brant is made up almost exclusively of farmers. At that time there was not one tractor in the township, and yet that township made the largest per capita subscription to the victory loan campaign in 1918. That was because they did not have gasoline bills to pay.
Three dollar wheat.

But wheat was just as high in every other part of Canada. That is the township in which I live, in which I was born, and in which my father and my grandfather pioneered. Hon. members across the way have the habit of digging up sordid things in this country. Apparently the hon. member for North Battleford (Mrs. Nielsen) quickly became afflicted with the disease because of her close association with them. In doing this, I do not think they offer a very good example of good citizenship. They bring all these things out of the gutter with all their filth, degredation and squalour and hold them up to society as an example of Canadian citizenship. I do not think they are doing this country the service they should be doing as hon. members. I have in my hand a resume of the progress which has been made since the

Special War Revenue Act
first of the century under the so-called profit system, which my hon. friends opposite claim has broken down because of the many abuses.
Does it show the debts?

I have a list of the debts, and I should like to show what we have purchased with some of those debts. This shows what has taken place in the United States, but it is also characteristic of Canada, although to a smaller degree. At the beginning of the century the United States had 8,000 automobiles; to-day they have 25,000,000. At the beginning of the century they had 1,000,000 telephones; to-day they have 20,400,000.
Twenty million unemployed.

In 1900 there were 4,400,000 security holders; in 1941 there are 16,000,000. In 1900 there were 16,000,000 savings accounts; to-day there are 46,000,000. In 1920 there were only 1.000 radio sets; in 1941 there are 43,000,000. That shows the rate at which we have been travelling. Hon. members will ask what this has to do with the gasoline tax. Perhaps my argument is not relevant, but I think it is time someone drew attention to the weaknesses of the arguments of hon. members opposite. I do not speak very often, and I think it is time that these members should be told to analyse themselves. I sometimes wonder whether they are proud of themselves as Canadian citizens when they read their own speeches. After all, we have accomplished a great deal by our present system; but when they endeavour to bring out the inferior things of life and set them up as examples of Canadian citizenship, they are doing a disservice to Canada.
I believe I am a fairly representative farmer of the Dominion of Canada, and I think I can interpret the opinion of the average farmer. He wants to do his part; he does not ask for sympathy. He wants to share and share alike with the burden that has to be borne; he does not want to feel that he is any less important than any other class of our people. The average farmer has more of the old pioneering blood in his veins than any other class. Unfortunately, especially in the western provinces, there are some who have not been long enough in this country to become acclimatized to some of the rigours of life. They are ready to squeal and complain when faced with difficulty, and they try to offer their views to those of us who have a background of 150 years in Canada.

Perhaps I should take the advice of the speaker who just preceded me. I am not a farmer; I have never worked the
soil, but I have been adopted by a constituency which is ninety-eight per cent rural. Therefore I think it is my duty to voice their sentiments. The hon. member for Brant (Mr. Wood) is quite fortunate in not having received any complaints. My constituency does not contain any great farms like those in western Canada, but I have received letters from some farmers complaining that this new tax will foe a burden, although only a small one. I understand the difficulties facing the minister in connection with the granting of rebates to farmers, and I sympathize with his position. However, the sympathy which I feel for him is more than balanced by the sympathy I have for the farmers in my constituency. The lot of the farmer, in both western and eastern Canada, was far from satisfactory during the years of the depression, when the position of all our population was not so good. What do we see to-day? Because of the industrial boom due to the war effort, our labouring classes are having their positions bettered day by day. Unfortunately we cannot say the same for the farmer. Any new tax that affects the farmer is not for the good of the country, nor is it conducive to sound economy. Therefore I wish to register my deep regret that the minister could not work out some plan which would have relieved the farmers of this new burden.

Why should the people of the maritime provinces have to pay two or three cents more a gallon for their gasoline than the people in the other provinces? There must be discrimination. I know this is a provincial matter, but the minister should take it up with the provinces with a view to having a level price for gasoline in all the provinces. We pay a tax of ten cents a gallon in New Brunswick, while in most of the other provinces the tax is seven cents. In Ontario it is eight cents. With this federal tax we shall be paying a tax of thirteen cents a gallon in New Brunswick. Will the provincial governments have to pay this tax on gasoline used in road work?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is not intended that the provincial governments shall be taxed. That will be covered in the bill. My hon. friend asked, why should the maritime provinces pay a higher gasoline tax than other provinces? It would be impossible for us to graduate our tax to accord with the taxes in the different provinces. The hon. gentleman will realize that we could not do that.

Has the minister ever
tried to get the maritime provinces to level up their provincial tax?
Special War Revenue Act

If the bill is going to
provide for exemption for the provinces from this tax and for the tax being collected at the refineries, certainly we are setting up some machinery which will provide for exemptions under this legislation, and if we are going to provide for exemptions for particular bodies, why should we not do the same thing for the farmers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As to setting up machinery, the matter is easily arranged.

I had not intended to speak again on exemption for farmers from the payment of this tax on gasoline, but I feel I must say a word in view of the objections which the Minister of Finance has stated to granting any rebate to the farmer. He has spoken of the frauds that are perpetrated in connection with rebates. I must be in a very fortunate position in that respect, because in the two ridings bordering on Ottawa I had the honour of being magistrate for five years, and during all that time there were only two prosecutions for tax evasions. There are, of course, abuses in connection with all legislation, but they must be considered in connection with the amount of revenue to be derived from the taxing legislation. The minister would not say that there should be no legislation restricting the sale of alcohol because of an occasional bootlegger.
We have heard a great deal said in this house this session about the sad plight of agriculture. It has been pointed out that thirtydive per cent of our population are getting only eleven per cent of the national income. Time and again it has been stated in this house that the farmer is not only a war casualty but also an economic casualty. We have had measures to bonus agricultural products, such as wheat, cheese and bacon. We have heard pleas in this house with regard to the scarcity of farm labour and the high cost of production for the farmer. Power implements are of great assistance to the farmer when labour is as scarce as it is at the present time. The hon. member for Fort William said that he had not much sympathy for the farmer who was not prepared to go back to the horse-and-buggy days and drive a team, but has he ever paid much attention to the class of people who are staying on the farm to-day? It is the older people who are staying on the farm. The younger people are gravitating to the cities to go into war industries or into the army, and that makes farm labour scarce. I believe it is our bounden duty to assist the farmer to get his work done with as little hand labour as possible. We are doing much to help him in other fields, and is this not another way in which 
we could help him even though there should be a small percentage of evasions of the tax?

I am sure that no member of this committee could have listened to the Minister of Finance giving the reasons which finally induced the government to impose this tax without feeling the sincerity of the words he uttered. I suggest to the hon. member for Weybum that he does our western people a disservice in misinterpreting the reasons which the minister gave to the committee and doubting his sincerity. It tends to block rather than to assist the work of this committee to suggest that the minister means more than he intended to mean in the statement be made with regard to the difficulties which have presented themselves and will in all likelihood continue to present themselves in the matter of exemptions from a tax such as this. The hon. member for Weyburn, coming as I do from Saskatchewan, knows that in the early stages of exemption from the gasoline tax certain men attempted to evade the tax. As has been pointed out, there have been a number of prosecutions, and I have no doubt that the provincial authorities will soon achieve a general application of the law without infractions and without the necessity of prosecutions such as the minister has mentioned. I for one realize fully the difficulties which the minister has pointed out. He has attempted to weigh the difficulties of granting exemption to the classes referred to, particularly farmers and fishermen, against the difficulties of not granting any exemptions and of having to extract this particular tax from those two vocations.
At the expense of irritating an hon. member with whom I seldom disagree, the hon. member for Brant, and also the hon. member for Fort William, I may say that I am quite in disagreement with their suggestion that we can turn back the hands of the clock and that our farmers can go back to the horse-and-buggy days of farming with any degree of success. That is an impossibility and one which we should not encourage because it is against the true interests of agriculture. Agriculture is no different from any other industry in this respect, that if those engaged in that industry are to enjoy a reasonable degree of prosperity in comparison with the rest of Canadians they must adopt efficient and progressive means of lowering their costs of production. We have heard on more than one occasion that there should be parity of prices as between agricultural products and the commodities the farmer buys. We can never accomplish that by pouring out bonuses to the farmer. There is only one true way in

Special War Revenue Act
which we can accomplish it. To pour bonuses out of the public treasury only means that in turn they must be collected by way of taxation from other classes, and we all know that in the present set-up the primary producer, having regard to his particular position in our economic whole, simply has no capacity to pass those taxes on. The rest of us, the professional classes, and the manufacturer and even labour to-day, have the opportunity of passing those taxes on to somebody else. But the farmer is at the bottom of the heap, and he finds it impossible to pass this or any other tax on to anybody else. If the question is studied fairly, it will be found that parity can never be achieved by pouring moneys out of the dominion treasury. I suggest that the true economy to be recognized, under the necessity with which the farmer and other primary producers are faced, is to attempt to apply the method of reducing, so far as possible, the cost of the commodities which they must purchase.
This particular tax, of course, is a direct tax upon every consumer of gasoline. I do not know why the minister exempted certain grades of distillate. He mentioned that the reason was that no tax is wholly equitable, the most equitable, I think he said, is the income tax. I believe, however, he will agree with me that one could not reasonably impose upon people with gray hair an income tax in a greater amount than on people who happened to have brown hair.
Or no hair at all.

Or no hair at all; if that were the situation, I would claim exemption. But I point out with all respect and deference to the minister that that is exactly what is being done in the case of this particular tax. In Canada, not only in the west but in the east, there has been a marked turning to tractor farming. This is not only a western question; as hon. members well know, in Ontario the use of tractors on the land is increasing rapidly. The hon. member for Carleton has pointed that out. In western Canada the younger farmer is studying his calling from a slightly different angle than that of his father. He proceeds on the basis of extreme efficiency and low cost of production, and the use of the tractor is enabling the young man in western Canada to continue in the vocation which he believes he can master on an economic basis, producing at a price which will enable him to sell in the world's market. We have all through Canada the same trend, and nothing that we can say will stop it.
Therefore, while realizing the difficulties with which the minister has contended in trying to make this tax fair, and realizing how difficult it is for the government or for this committee to suggest concrete ways of helping agriculture, I suggest that the exemption of agriculturists, and indeed, fishermen, from this particular tax would be a concrete way of helping these classes of producers. I do not believe that since I have come to this house I have ever heard a voice raised in an attempt to argue that agriculture is not in an unfair position in comparison with the other economic sections of our community. The difficulty has been to devise suitable ways of helping the agriculturist, and here, at least, is one. Even though the farmer uses his car occasionally for pleasure, there is probably no individual who owns a car who uses it less for that purpose and more on business than the farmer, because his present plight will not permit him to take any long jaunts for his own recreation. Even though a few who should pay the tax might escape it, I suggest to the minister that the lesser of two evils is to devise ways and means of implementing the principle of exemption of farmers and fishermen.
When this tax was imposed, the price of gasoline in certain parts of Ontario, and certainly in metropolitan Toronto, jumped five cents. Can the minister give us any explanation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have no information about that.
The companies were giving a rebate of two cents, but when the tax was imposed they stopped giving that rebate, and the price jumped five cents.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have no information about that.

I should like to compliment the leader of the opposition upon his suggestion that the whole oil industry should be nationalized. It seems that the influence of the group on his left is beginning to have some effect upon the leader of the opposition.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I was just flirting with the idea.

It has been said that this three cent tax is only small, but it is a fifteen per cent increase in the cost of the fuel, and the price of the engine which is burning that fuel has gone up to the producer twenty per cent since the war started. Therefore the tax really amounts to something, especially in view of the farmers' income at this time. The
Special War Revenue Act

minister raised the exemption in respect of the defence tax from $600 to $660. I believe everybody in the house complimented him upon that action, and many desired that the exemption should be raised to $750. The average farm income in Saskatchewan for the past four years has been away below $600. That is proved by the appendix to the Sirois report. Yet we are imposing additional taxation on these people who have less than $600 a year, a sum which includes the value of the products used by the farmers from their own farms. This is unfair. In another aspect, also, it is unfair, because most of the large farmers and the insurance companies or corporations that own big tracts of land in the west are using diesel tractors, and are thus able to produce more cheaply than the ordinary small farmer who operates with a gasoline engine.
To my mind our entire agricultural policy at this time is a mistaken one. We are raising the cost of producing agricultural products, and so are creating a shortage of these products. Sooner or later, and it will not be very long in Canada, this shortage will occur. Already we have had to reduce the consumption of pork for domestic use, and so far as dairy produce is concerned, I believe we shall have a shortage within another year. Every time you add to the cost of production you increase the tendency to lessen production. The government would be well-advised to reconsider this tax. Their chief argument has been the difficulty in administering exemptions. But in view of the fact that the provinces are rebating the gasoline tax under much the same circumstances, I do not see why the dominion government cannot do the same. They might at least give the system a trial for a year. As time goes on, Great Britain will require more and more food products. It is our duty to produce these, and I hope the government's attitude towards agriculture will not be such as will make it impossible for us to supply Britain with the products she will need during the next two or three years.

I have pointed out that in my judgment this tax is fair, but the total tax, federal and provincial, is oppressive, and a good case has been made out for that.
I have suggested to the minister a course which may or may not have merit. Having in mind that he has made or offered to make an arrangement with the provinces in respect of two other invasions of tax fields, I should like very much to have his comments with regard to my proposals.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I would echo what the hon. gentleman has said, 
especially in respect of the provinces down by the sea. Thirteen cents a gallon is oppressive. An arrangement might be made by negotiation to iron that out, and I think the minister ought to take the lead. He cannot do it to-night, but he can do it in course of time. Let us be put on the same level. Personally I do not object to the three cent tax; it is another contribution to the war, but let us get this matter on an equitable basis.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know how to do that. I have listened to the suggestion of the hon. member for Essex East, that we pay the provinces to get out of the field-
Give them some compensation, if necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, three cents a gallon means $25,000,000; we would have to pay the provinces that $25,000,000, which would leave us just where we were before.
Only to some provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To give anything less would not mean much.

The hon. member for Essex East suggested that the gasoline tax was originally imposed in Ontario for the purpose of building roads; he also said that road building in Ontario had stopped or practically stopped, and that the cost of maintenance of roads is now down to a minimum. If that is true, what is happening to the eight cents a gallon which is being collected by the province at this time? I think we would be well advised, as members of this house, to urge on the provincial governments that they do something to cut down their own expenses and, therefore, reduce the necessity for the gasoline tax that they collect at the present time.

I would point out that it is unfair that government officials driving round in government cars should be exempt from this tax and that farmers should not be. In New Brunswick we have the lowest farm income of any province, and we have a thirteen cent gasoline tax.

I should like to ask the minister a question. He did not answer me in connection with the question of collection of the tax. The provinces now have the machinery for its collection. It is proposed that the federal government shall collect this tax, with all the ramifications involved. Why was it decided that the tax should be col-

Special War Revenue Act
lected from the refinery and not through the agencies of the various provinces who now have the machinery?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have the machinery also. The sales tax organization is in existence; the excise division of the Department of National Revenue is-I was going to say a perfect organization-an efficient organization.

But how are you going to find out how much gasoline each province uses? For example, a road inspector for Ontario is going along in his car; he stops at a gasoline station and gets so many gallons. Here is a tractor on the road; it gets so much gasoline. Here are various other provincial vehicles, motorcycles; all these are going to be free from the gasoline tax. How are you going to find out what those exemptions will be?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Section 105 of the Special War Revenue Act states:	'
A refund of the amount of taxes paid (under certain parts) may be granted to a manufacturer, producer, wholesaler, jobber or other dealer on goods sold to His Majesty in the right of the government of any province of Canada, if the said goods are purchased by His Majesty for any purpose other than purposes of resale or of any railway, commission, board or public utility which is operated by or under the authority of the legislature or the lieutenant governor in council of the province.
The point is, refunds of sales tax are made to manufacturers now upon production of evidence that the sale was made to his majesty in the right of a province.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: What is proposed to be done to check the use of provincial government gasoline, because it is a fact that it is not all used exclusively in connection with the business of the government as such? There is a tremendous amount which is used in flying round the country that is not business.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Very small.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Well,	it
is substantial, and the government will hear about that if it does not take some steps to check t'he use by the provincial governments, and especially by their officials. Every provincial government has an army of cars; everyone has a car, just as everyone in the federal service has a car. If I understand the situation correctly, that evil, if I may call it that, of providing motor cars for all government officials from the Atlantic to the Pacific has grown substantially in the last five or six years. There are too many cars provided by governments for their officials.
Nobody walks to-day. This is particularly true in the militia. Let me tell the minister something. Just opposite my home is a military hospital. There are never less than ten cars on the street in front of my home or in the yard of the hospital, and I have never yet seen anyone walk to that hospital except a buck private. I suggest that when the minister has this provision put through, as he seems bound to do, the excise division should set up some check on the provincial government's consumption of gasoline. Perhaps he will not lose as much revenue as I think he is losing to-day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They check that now.

Why does the minister
propose to exempt provincial governments and their employees?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
What
contribution do they make to the war?

There is no equitable principle behind such an exemption. One province may have a small army of such public servants, and their ratio of expenditure for gasoline may be entirely out of keeping with that of another province, and just to that extent by exempting it we are going to be grossly unfair. Why not let them pay their shot, take care of it themselves just as fishermen, farmers and all other drivers of cars do?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Quite
right.
And the brass-hats too.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I can consider that, but it
would mean the introduction of a new principle; we would have protests from every province. I do not know of a single instance where the federal government steps into a province and lays a tax on the province which will be paid out of the taxes that it imposes on its people. It would be introducing a new principle.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Let the
minister sleep on it.
The minister said that the tax is going to be collected from the refineries.

Eleven o'clock.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.

Wednesday, May 21, 1941.
